lead: Controllability and observability are two structural questions about a state model. Controllability asks whether the input u can move every state variable. Observability asks whether the output y can reveal every initial state. A system can be stable and still fail either test. The tests use matrix rank: Q<sub>c</sub> = [B AB ... A<sup>n−1</sup>B] for controllability and Q<sub>o</sub> = [C; CA; ...; CA<sup>n−1</sup>] for observability. Engineers use these checks before state feedback, pole placement and state estimation, where an uncontrollable or unobservable state silently blocks the design.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.2 and Chapter 6.3, plus the idea of matrix rank.

sections.h3: Controllability and the Qc rank test

blocks.text: Write a linear time-invariant (LTI) state model as xdot = A x + B u, y = C x + D u. x is the n×1 state vector, u is the m×1 input vector, y is the p×1 output vector, A is n×n, B is n×m, C is p×n and D is p×m. The pair (A, B) is controllable when u can drive x from any initial value to any chosen final value in finite time.

The controllability matrix is Q<sub>c</sub> = [B AB A²B ... A<sup>n−1</sup>B]. It has n rows and nm columns. Its columns are B, AB, and so on up to n−1 powers of A. Rank means the number of independent rows or columns. The test is rank(Q<sub>c</sub>) = n. If rank(Q<sub>c</sub>) < n, some state combination cannot be reached, whatever input is applied.
Q<sub>c</sub> = [B  AB  A<sup>2</sup>B  ...  A<sup>n−1</sup>B],   rank(Q<sub>c</sub>) = n
blocks.where: A is n×n; B is n×m; n is the number of states; m is the number of inputs; rank(Q<sub>c</sub>) is the number of independent columns of Q<sub>c</sub>.

items: Count the states n from A.
Form the n blocks B, AB, ..., A<sup>n−1</sup>B.
Place them side by side as columns of Q<sub>c</sub>.
Find rank(Q<sub>c</sub>). Rank n means controllable; rank below n means not controllable.

blocks.text: For one input (m = 1), Q<sub>c</sub> is square n×n, so det(Q<sub>c</sub>) ≠ 0 is the quick test. The figure at the end of this chapter shows the two-state model used in the worked example: u enters x2, the states are coupled, and x1 reaches y.

sections.h3: Observability and the Qo rank test

blocks.text: The pair (A, C) is observable when y over a finite time interval is enough to determine the initial state x(0). If two initial states produce the same output for all time, the hidden difference cannot be seen. The output is the only evidence of that hidden state.

The observability matrix stacks rows: Q<sub>o</sub> = [C; CA; ...; CA<sup>n−1</sup>]. It has pn rows and n columns, where p is the number of outputs. The test is rank(Q<sub>o</sub>) = n. If rank(Q<sub>o</sub>) < n, some state combination cannot be recovered from the output. For one output (p = 1), Q<sub>o</sub> is square n×n, so det(Q<sub>o</sub>) ≠ 0 proves observability.

blocks.where: C is p×n; A is n×n; n is the number of states; p is the number of outputs; the semicolons stack rows.

blocks.text: Duality: (A, B) is controllable iff (A<sup>T</sup>, B<sup>T</sup>) is observable, with B<sup>T</sup> as the output matrix. The PBH test checks rank [λI − A  B] = n for every eigenvalue λ of A for controllability, and rank [λI − A; C] = n for observability. λ is an eigenvalue of A and I is the n×n identity matrix. Only a few universities teach PBH in detail; the Q<sub>c</sub> and Q<sub>o</sub> rank tests are the standard exam route.

Stability and controllability answer different questions. Stability says a disturbed state returns to rest by itself. Controllability says the input can place the state wherever you want. A stable mode can be completely disconnected from the input, so it decays but cannot be steered.

Example: A = diag(−1, −2), B = [0; 1]. The eigenvalues are −1 and −2, so the system is stable. AB = [0; −2], and Q<sub>c</sub> = [B AB] = [[0, 0], [1, −2]]. The two columns are proportional; rank(Q<sub>c</sub>) = 1 < 2. The input moves x2 only. State x1 has no path from u, so it is uncontrollable even though it decays to zero.

The same reading applies to observability. A stable hidden state can fade away, so the output looks well behaved, yet the initial value of that state cannot be recovered. Before pole placement, check Qc; state feedback cannot move an uncontrollable state. Before building an observer, check Qo; an unobservable state cannot be estimated. The next chapter uses these tests directly for state feedback and pole placement.

figure.caption: Signal-flow view of the worked example: input u enters state x2, the states feed each other, and only x1 reaches output y. The values on the edges are the entries of A, B and C.

spec.aria: A directed graph with input u entering state x2, x2 and x1 coupled by gains 1 and −2, a self-loop −3 on x2, and x1 feeding output y.

examples.question: For A = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]], B = [0; 1] and C = [1, 0], use rank tests to decide controllability and observability. Give the determinants.
steps: Q<sub>c</sub> = [B AB] = [[0, 1], [1, −3]]. det(Q<sub>c</sub>) = (0)(−3) − (1)(1) = −1. Rank(Q<sub>c</sub>) = 2 = n, so controllable.
Q<sub>o</sub> = [C; CA] = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]. det(Q<sub>o</sub>) = (1)(1) − (0)(0) = 1. Rank(Q<sub>o</sub>) = 2 = n, so observable.
examples.answer: The system is controllable (rank Qc = 2) and observable (rank Qo = 2); det Qc = −1 and det Qo = 1.
examples.check:
A = [[0, 1], [-2, -3]]
B = [[0], [1]]
C = [[1, 0]]

def mul(X, Y):
    r = len(X)
    c = len(Y[0])
    k = len(Y)
    Z = [[0]*c for _ in range(r)]
    for i in range(r):
        for j in range(c):
            Z[i][j] = sum(X[i][t]*Y[t][j] for t in range(k))
    return Z

def det2(M):
    return M[0][0]*M[1][1] - M[0][1]*M[1][0]

def rank2(M):
    d = det2(M)
    if d != 0:
        return 2
    for row in M:
        if any(v != 0 for v in row):
            return 1
    return 0

AB = mul(A, B)
Qc = [[B[i][0], AB[i][0]] for i in range(2)]
CA = mul(C, A)
Qo = [C[0], CA[0]]
rQc = rank2(Qc)
rQo = rank2(Qo)
print(rQc)
print(rQo)
print(det2(Qc))
print(det2(Qo))

traps: Always form all n blocks before deciding; a single block can prove controllability only in the special case where B alone already has rank n, which is rare.
Qc is n×nm, not always square. For m > 1, rank n is the test; determinant exists only for m = 1.
Stable does not mean controllable. Diag(−1, −2) with B = [0; 1] is stable but rank Qc = 1 < 2.
Qc stacks B, AB, ... as columns. Qo stacks C, CA, ... as rows. Reversing this gives wrong dimensions.
Controllability and observability are separate. Duality compares (A, B) with (A<sup>T</sup>, B<sup>T</sup>), not with the same system's (A, C).

quiz.q: Define controllability of an LTI state model.
quiz.a: The input can drive the state from any initial value to any chosen final value in finite time.

quiz.q: Write the rank tests for controllability and observability.
quiz.a: rank Qc = n with Qc = [B AB ... A<sup>n−1</sup>B]; rank Qo = n with Qo = [C; CA; ...; CA<sup>n−1</sup>].

quiz.q: Why does rank Qc < n mean some state cannot be reached?
quiz.a: The columns span only a proper subspace of state space; directions outside that span have no input path.
AB = [1;0]. Qc = [[1,1],[0,0]]. det = 0, rank = 1 < 2, so not controllable.

quiz.q: Give a stable but uncontrollable second-order system and prove it.
quiz.a: A = diag(−1,−2), B = [0;1]. Eigenvalues −1,−2 are stable. AB = [0;−2], Qc = [[0,0],[1,−2]], rank = 1 < 2, so uncontrollable.

quiz.q: For A = [[0,1],[−2,−3]] and C = [1,1], test observability.
quiz.a: CA = [−2,−2]. Qo = [[1,1],[−2,−2]]. det = 0, rank = 1 < 2, so not observable.

quiz.q: State duality and explain its use in exams.
quiz.a: (A,B) controllable iff (A<sup>T</sup>,B<sup>T</sup>) observable with B<sup>T</sup> as output matrix. A controllability calculation can answer an observability question after transposing.

beyond: Not for the exam. Minimal realization removes uncontrollable and unobservable parts; Kalman decomposition shows the four parts separately. PBH connects these rank tests to eigenvalues and is useful in research. In practice, sensor placement and actuator placement use observability and controllability to avoid hidden states. Search terms: Kalman decomposition, minimal realization, PBH test, observability Gramian.
